reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: A severe autosomal recessive cholestasis caused by biallelic mutations in NR1H4, which encodes the farnesoid X receptor (FXR)
Presents in the neonatal period with rapidly progressive cholestasis and a low or normal gamma-glutamyl transferase
A striking early feature is a severe vitamin K-independent coagulopathy, reflecting profoundly impaired hepatic synthetic function
Serum alpha-fetoprotein is characteristically very high
FXR is the master nuclear bile acid sensor regulating bile acid synthesis and transport; its loss impairs canalicular bile salt export (BSEP) and disrupts bile acid homeostasis
Liver failure often develops in infancy, and the disease tends to be more aggressive than other PFIC subtypes
Management is supportive with fat-soluble vitamins, correction of coagulopathy, and early consideration of liver transplantation, which is often required
reference.pathophysiology: PFIC type 5 results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in NR1H4, encoding the farnesoid X receptor, the principal nuclear receptor sensing bile acids within the hepatocyte. FXR normally regulates transcription of genes controlling bile acid synthesis, conjugation, and canalicular export, including the bile salt export pump. Its absence causes failure of canalicular bile salt transport, accumulation of toxic bile acids, and disrupted bile acid homeostasis, producing severe neonatal cholestasis with a low/normal GGT, marked coagulopathy, high alpha-fetoprotein, and early progression to liver failure.
additionalInvestigations: Serum bile acids and gamma-glutamyl transferase (characteristically low/normal GGT)
Liver biopsy with immunostaining showing absent BSEP/FXR expression
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and liver synthetic markers
Genetic testing of NR1H4 and the PFIC gene panel
redFlags: Severe coagulopathy unresponsive to vitamin K with bleeding
Ascites, hypoglycaemia, or encephalopathy indicating decompensation
reference.prognosis: PFIC type 5 is one of the most severe cholestatic syndromes, frequently causing liver failure in infancy and requiring early liver transplantation; without transplantation the prognosis is poor.
pitfalls: Attributing the coagulopathy to vitamin K deficiency alone and expecting a response to replacement
Interpreting a low GGT as excluding significant cholestasis
Delaying referral for transplant assessment given the aggressive course
Overlooking the very high alpha-fetoprotein as a diagnostic clue
